plain: Vercel is the place where your website lives so everyone can see it. You have your project's files saved online, on GitHub, and Vercel takes them, builds them, and publishes them at an address you can send over WhatsApp. Think of it as a rented storefront on a busy street: you put what's visible inside, they provide the storefront, the lighting, the shutter, and the security guard. Every time you change something, the storefront updates itself within a minute, and if the change looks bad you can go back to yesterday's with one button.

account.free: Yes, there's a free plan called Hobby. It gives unlimited websites, 100 GB of traffic a month, automatic security lock (HTTPS), free custom domains, and preview URLs. Enough to learn, for a portfolio, and to show your idea to ten people. Two conditions: the Hobby plan is for personal, non-commercial use (if your site makes money, Vercel will ask you to move to Pro), and you can only publish 100 times a day. The Pro plan costs $20 a month per person, roughly €19 a month, and also separately charges for anything you use above what's included. Prices change often: check vercel.com/pricing yourself before paying.
steps: Sign in with GitHub, not email

On vercel.com click 'Sign Up' top right and choose 'Continue with GitHub'. Even though you could sign in with email, do it with GitHub: Vercel needs to read your code from there, and this way it's connected from minute one. If you don't have a GitHub account yet, create one first; it's free and it's where the AI will be saving your files.
Choose Hobby and say it's personal

It'll ask 'What best describes you?'. Check 'I'm working on personal projects'. That puts you on the Hobby plan, which is free. No card required. Give your account a name, e.g. your own name; it'll be part of your sites' addresses.

Vercel sends you to GitHub with a screen saying 'Install Vercel' and offers 'All repositories' or 'Only select repositories'. Choose 'Only select repositories' and check the project you're working on. A repository (repository: your project's folder saved online, with its change history) is each of your ideas.

On the dashboard click 'Add New...' top right and then 'Project'. The 'Import Git Repository' list appears. Next to your project, click 'Import'. If it doesn't show up, click 'Adjust GitHub App Permissions' and add it.
STOP HERE: paste the environment variables BEFORE publishing

Before clicking the black 'Deploy' button, open the 'Environment Variables' section right above it. It's a dropdown almost everyone skips, and that's why almost everyone fails the first time. Open the .env.local file on your computer and paste each name into 'Key' and each value into 'Value', one by one. Trick: you can copy the entire .env.local file and paste it all at once into the Key field; Vercel splits it into rows on its own.
Deploy and wait about a minute and a half

Click 'Deploy'. You'll see a screen with black text scrolling: it's the 'Build Log', the diary of what the machine is doing with your code. If confetti shows up, it's published. If 'Build Failed' shows up in red, you haven't broken anything: the previous code is still online and you just need to read the error.
Save the address and test it on your phone

Click 'Continue to Dashboard' and at the top you'll see your address, something like my-project.vercel.app. Copy it with the 'Visit' button or the copy icon. Open it on your phone using mobile data, not home wifi: that way you confirm it's really on the internet and not just working on your own computer.
account.warning: Your first deploy is going to fail, and almost always for the same reason: the keys. The file where you keep your passwords and service keys is called .env.local and is deliberately excluded from what gets uploaded to the internet. In other words: your code reaches Vercel, but your keys do NOT. Vercel starts your site, the site asks for the database key or the AI key, doesn't find it, and crashes. It's not a mistake by you or the AI: it's by design. You have to copy those keys into Vercel by hand, and then republish after copying them. That's it.

first: Go to vercel.com with 'Continue with GitHub' and check 'I'm working on personal projects' to stay on the free plan.
'Add New...' → 'Project' → find your project in the list and click 'Import'.

Before touching 'Deploy', open 'Environment Variables', open your .env.local file, copy it entirely, and paste it into the 'Key' field. Check that all the rows were created and no stray quote marks got in.
Click 'Deploy' and wait. If it turns red, copy the last 20 lines of the log and paste them to the AI saying: 'this fails when deploying to Vercel, what do I do?'.

Once it works, go to 'Settings' → 'Environment Variables' and check that every variable has all three boxes checked: Production, Preview, and Development. Then go back to 'Deployments', three dots '⋯' on the latest one, 'Redeploy'.
shortcuts: Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac)

Opens the dashboard's command search. Type a project's name and jump to it, or type 'env' and it takes you to the variables. With four projects it already saves more time than using the mouse. If it doesn't respond in your browser, use the search bar at the top: it does the same thing.
'Deployments' tab

The list of every time your site has been published, newest first, with the time, the branch, and the status: 'Ready', 'Error', or 'Building'. It's your history and your time machine. You come here every time something goes wrong.
'Visit' button

Top right of the project. Opens the published site in a new tab. Always use it instead of typing the address by hand: that way you see exactly the version that's online, not one cached in your browser's memory.
Three dots '⋯' → 'Redeploy'

On any deployment in the list. Rebuilds the site with the SAME code. It's the button to press whenever you change an environment variable. When it asks, uncheck 'Use existing Build Cache': it takes an extra minute but stops it reusing stale junk.
Three dots '⋯' → 'Instant Rollback' or 'Promote to Production'

On an old deployment marked 'Ready'. Restores your public site to that version in seconds, without building anything. It's the panic button. Depending on your plan and the dashboard version you'll see one name or the other; for you they do the same thing.
'Settings' → 'Environment Variables'
The key cabinet. Here you add, edit, and delete environment variables, and here you set which environments each one applies to. You'll come here more than anywhere else in Vercel.
'Logs' tab

What happens to your site while people use it: every visit, every AI call, every error. If the page loads but the button does nothing, the answer is here. On the free plan these logs are kept for a short time, so check them right after the failure, not tomorrow.
Ctrl+F inside the log and search for 'Error:'
A build log has 300 lines and only one matters. Search for 'Error:' and keep the FIRST one that appears, not the last. The ones below are usually consequences of the first.
'Settings' → 'Domains'
Where you connect your own domain, like mystore.com, to the site you've already published. Also where you check whether the domain is set up correctly or shows 'Invalid Configuration'.
Vercel's automatic comment on GitHub

When you push a new branch, Vercel automatically writes a comment on GitHub with a 'Visit Preview' link. That link is the test version of that branch. Copy it and send it over WhatsApp so people can give feedback without touching the real site.
daily: Adding a new key and republishing. Every time the AI tells you 'now put your X key in the .env.local file', you have to do the same thing twice: on your computer and in Vercel ('Settings' → 'Environment Variables' → 'Add Another'). And then 'Deployments' → '⋯' → 'Redeploy'. Without that redeploy, the variable exists but your site still can't see it: variables get frozen at build time.

Understanding the three checkboxes: Production, Preview, and Development. When creating a variable, Vercel lets you choose where it applies. Production is your real site, the one on your domain. Preview is the test versions of each branch. Development is your own computer. Rule to start with: check all three. Once you're actually taking money, split them: Stripe's test key (sk_test_...) in Preview and Development, and the real one (sk_live_...) only in Production.

Working with branches so you don't break what works. Tell the AI: 'create a new branch called home-redesign and work there.' When you push it, Vercel publishes that branch at a separate address, something like myapp-git-home-redesign-yourusername.vercel.app. Your real site never knows. Once you like it, merge the branch into main and only then does it go live.

Reading the log when something fails, without understanding it. You don't need to know what it says. Go into the red deployment, click 'Build Logs', search for 'Error:', copy that line and the ten around it, and paste them to the AI. 90% of failures get fixed in one back-and-forth.

Rolling back when you've messed something up. 'Deployments' → find the last good one → '⋯' → 'Instant Rollback'. Your site is back to normal in 10 seconds. Important warning: that does NOT fix the code, only what's visible. Next time the AI pushes something, the bug returns. After the rollback you have to actually fix it.

Watching who's coming in and what's breaking live. 'Logs' tab. Filter by 'Status' 500 to see only the errors. If your AI assistant sometimes responds and sometimes doesn't, here you'll see if it's timing out or the key is wrong.

Watching your spend before it starts watching you. 'Settings' → 'Usage' in your account. Check the traffic and function calls. If your site suddenly gets popular, this is where you find out before a bill surprises you. On Hobby you can't be charged unexpectedly, it just throttles you; on Pro you do pay for the overage.

templates.name: The two key lists: .env.local and .env.example
templates.what: This template solves 80% of deployment problems. There are two sibling files. The first, .env.local, has your real keys and never leaves your computer. The second, .env.example, has the same names but no values, and it DOES get uploaded: it's so you (and the AI) know at a glance which keys need to be copied into Vercel. Works for any project: a store, an assistant, a form-based site.
templates.how: 1) Ask the AI: 'create me a .env.example file with all the variables this project uses, without values'. 2) Open .env.local on your computer and fill in the real values. 3) Check that .gitignore contains the line .env*.local; if it's not there, tell the AI to add it. 4) In Vercel, 'Settings' → 'Environment Variables', copy the entire content of .env.local and paste it into the 'Key' field: Vercel splits it into rows automatically. 5) Check all three boxes: Production, Preview, and Development. 6) 'Deployments' → '⋯' → 'Redeploy'.
fill: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL
Your Supabase project's address (Project Settings → API). Starts with https:// and ends in .supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY
Supabase's public key, labeled 'anon public'. It's long and starts with eyJ
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY
Supabase's secret key, labeled 'service_role'. This one NEVER has NEXT_PUBLIC in front
OPENAI_API_KEY
Your OpenAI key (platform.openai.com → API keys). Starts with sk-
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
Your Stripe key. Use the test one (sk_test_) until you're ready to actually charge people
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL
On your computer: http://localhost:3000. On Vercel: your real address, https://yoursite.vercel.app or your domain
templates.code:
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# FILE 1  ·  .env.local
# Lives ONLY on your computer. Never uploaded to the internet.
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Database
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://abcdefghijklm.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.paste-yours-here
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.this-one-is-secret

# AI
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-paste-yours-here
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-paste-yours-here

# Payments (use the TEST ones until the very end)
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_paste-yours-here
NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_test_paste-yours-here
STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_paste-yours-here

# Your site's address. On your computer it's always this:
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=http://localhost:3000


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# FILE 2  ·  .env.example
# This one DOES get uploaded. Same names, zero values.
# It's the shopping list you take to Vercel.
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=
OPENAI_API_KEY=
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=
NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=
STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# FILE 3  ·  .gitignore
# Check it contains THESE lines. If not, your keys
# end up published on the internet for anyone to see.
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

templates.name: Health check page: /api/health
templates.what: A hidden page on your own site that tells you, at a glance, whether Vercel is seeing your keys or not. Saves you from the eternal question '​did I set it up right?'. It doesn't show the value of the keys, only whether they're present, how many characters they have, and the first 4, so you can check you didn't paste in one from a different service. It also tells you which environment you're in: production, preview, or development.
templates.how: 1) Tell the AI: 'create the file app/api/health/route.ts with this content' and paste the code. 2) Change the REQUIRED list to the names of YOUR variables. 3) Push the change. 4) Open yoursite.vercel.app/api/health in the browser. You'll see text with braces. If 'allGood' says true, your keys are there. If a name appears in 'missing', that variable isn't in Vercel, or isn't checked for that environment, or you haven't redeployed since adding it. 5) IMPORTANT: once you're done debugging, tell the AI to delete this file, or at least password-protect it. It's your utility closet, don't leave it open.
fill: The REQUIRED list
The exact names of your variables, exactly as written in .env.local, respecting capitalization
The file path
app/api/health/route.ts if you're using Next.js with the App Router. If your project is something else, ask the AI to adapt it
The address you open
Your domain + /api/health. Test it on a preview URL too, to check the Preview environment

templates.name: vercel.json: the deployment settings file
templates.what: A small file in your project's root where you tell Vercel four things: which country you want the machine in, how long your AI assistant is allowed to take to respond before it's cut off, and some basic security headers. Mostly useful if your audience is in Europe (by default Vercel puts you in the US) and if you use AI, since long responses get cut off after a few seconds.
templates.how: 1) Tell the AI: 'create me a vercel.json file at the root of the project with this content'. 2) Paste in the code. 3) If your project isn't Next.js, remove the "framework" line and let the AI adapt it. 4) Push the change; the deploy will happen on its own. 5) If the deploy fails with 'Invalid Configuration' or complains about maxDuration, remove that block and push again: duration limits vary by plan, and on the free one they're usually lower. 6) The fra1 region is Frankfurt, the closest of the usual ones to Europe; on the free plan you can only choose one region, and if it gives you trouble remove that line and it'll work the same, just a bit slower from Europe.
fill: "regions": ["fra1"]
fra1 is Frankfurt. If your audience is in Latin America or the US, use iad1 (Washington), which is the default
"maxDuration": 30
The seconds you give your AI assistant to respond. Raise it if it's cutting off, lower it to 10 if Vercel complains
"app/api/**/*.ts"
The folder where your functions live. If the AI put things somewhere else, have it adjust this

templates.name: Deployment fact sheet: what you paste to the AI every time
templates.what: A short text you fill in once per project and paste to the AI at the start of every work session. It avoids the most expensive vibe-coding problem: the AI assuming you're using something else, changing your variable names, or proposing settings from a different service. With this in front of it, the AI gets it right on the first try much more often.
templates.how: 1) Copy the block below into a note (Obsidian, Notes, a NOTES.md file inside the project). 2) Fill in the blanks with your real data, but NEVER paste a key's value there: only its name. 3) Every time you open a new conversation with the AI, paste the sheet into the first message. 4) Update it when you add a variable or change domains. If the AI proposes something that contradicts the sheet, tell it: 'that doesn't match my sheet, review it.'
fill: Project and what it does
One sentence. E.g.: handmade-candle store with cart and checkout
Name on Vercel and URL
As shown in the dashboard: my-store and my-store.vercel.app
Own domain
mystore.com if you have one, or 'not yet' if you don't
List of variables
Just the NAMES, comma-separated. Never the values
Main branch
Usually main. It's the one that goes live for real
Connected services
Supabase, OpenAI, Stripe, Resend... whatever you use
templates.code:
MY PROJECT'S FACT SHEET — paste at the start of every AI session

What it is: [one sentence on what the site does]
Built with: [Next.js / whatever the AI told you the first time]
Hosted on: Vercel, Hobby plan (free)
Project on Vercel: [my-project]
Public URL: [my-project.vercel.app]
Own domain: [mystore.com  ·  or: not yet]
Main branch: [main]

Environment variables it uses (names ONLY):
[NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY,
 SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL]

Connected services: [Supabase, OpenAI, Stripe]

HOW I WORK, respect this:
- I don't know how to code. Explain what each change does in one sentence.
- Give me complete files, not loose snippets.
- If a change needs a new environment variable, tell me
  the exact name and remind me to also add it in Vercel.
- Don't rename an existing variable without a warning.
- No keys written inside the code: always process.env.

errors: Translation: 'the Supabase address is missing'. This can show up with any service, just changing the name. It means that environment variable isn't reaching Vercel. Three causes, in this order: (1) you haven't created it in 'Settings' → 'Environment Variables'; (2) you created it but only checked for Production, and you're opening a preview; (3) you created it correctly but haven't redeployed. Variables are read at build time, not after. Fix: create or check the variable, check all three boxes, then 'Deployments' → '⋯' → 'Redeploy' with the cache unchecked.
Error: Environment Variable "OPENAI_API_KEY" references Secret "openai_api_key", which does not exist.

Shows up when the AI wrote an "env" block in your vercel.json with values starting with an @, like "@openai_api_key". It's an old way of doing things Vercel no longer uses. Fix: tell the AI 'remove the env block and the build.env block from my vercel.json, I manage variables from the Vercel dashboard.' Then set them by hand in 'Settings' → 'Environment Variables'. It's the classic error when copying a configuration from an old tutorial.
The site loads but shows blank, and the browser console says: undefined

Symptom: it works on your computer, on the internet the page is empty or the chat doesn't respond. Almost always it's the prefix. In Next.js, only variables whose name starts with NEXT_PUBLIC_ reach the browser; the rest stay on the server and from the browser they're undefined. If your code needs that variable in the browser, you have to rename it adding NEXT_PUBLIC_ in front, on your computer AND in Vercel, and redeploy. Watch out for the opposite trap: EVERYTHING with NEXT_PUBLIC_ is visible to anyone who opens your site. Never put secret keys or database passwords there.

Translation: 'can't find that file'. And the file is right there, you can see it. The reason is that your computer (Windows or Mac) treats uppercase and lowercase as the same, and Vercel's computers don't: to them header.tsx and Header.tsx are two different files. That's why it works at home and fails on publish. Fix: paste the error to the AI and say 'this only fails on Vercel, I think it's a capitalization issue in the file name, check what it's really called and how I'm calling it.' It's a two-minute fix that can cost you an afternoon if you don't know it exists.
Error: Command "npm run build" exited with 1

The generic error. It only means 'something broke while building the site' and it's never the real cause: it's the last line, the one saying the patient died, not why. Scroll up the log until you find the FIRST line that says 'Error:' or 'Type error:'. Copy that line and the ten around it. That's what you paste to the AI. If you paste only 'exited with 1', the AI can't guess anything and you'll waste time.

The site published fine, but it crashed internally when used. The build went well, so the problem isn't the code itself, it's something that only shows up running: a wrong key, a database table that doesn't exist, a service saying no. Go to the 'Logs' tab, filter by Status 500, and look for the message from that time. That message, not the 500, is what you paste to the AI. Remember on the free plan logs don't last long: check them right away.

Time ran out. Your site asked the AI or a database for something, the response took longer than allowed, and Vercel cut the call off. Happens a lot with AI assistants writing long responses. Two fixes, in this order: (1) ask the AI to use 'streaming' (a response delivered in chunks, written as it thinks); (2) raise maxDuration in vercel.json. On the free plan the ceiling is low, so streaming is the real fix, not the patch on the time limit.
Authentication Required · You need to be logged in to access this deployment

You open the preview URL you sent a friend and it asks them to log into Vercel. It's not broken: it's 'Deployment Protection', which keeps preview versions visible only to you. If you want to show it, you have two options: 'Settings' → 'Deployment Protection' and turn off 'Vercel Authentication' for previews, or generate a temporary link with 'Share' from the deployment itself. Think it through first: if that version has real customer data, better leave it protected.

prompts.name: Environment variable inventory before the first deploy
prompts.prompt: Act as the technical person helping me out. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn: I talk to you and you write the code. We're going to prepare my project to publish on Vercel, and I want to nail down the environment variables issue once and for all, because I know it's where everyone fails the first time. Do this in order and don't skip steps. First, review my ENTIRE project and make me a table with every environment variable the code uses: exact name respecting capitalization, what it's for in one plain-person sentence, which service it comes from and the exact screen in that service where I find it, whether it's secret or public, and whether it should carry the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix or not. Second, tell me which of those variables need a DIFFERENT value in production, in preview, and on my computer, and why; think especially about test keys versus real ones and the site's address. Third, create the complete .env.example file for me and check that .gitignore excludes .env.local; if it doesn't, fix it and warn me, because that means my keys might already be published. Fourth, give me the final list in a format ready to paste all at once into Vercel's Key field. Fifth, warn me about any variable whose value I need to generate myself or pay for. My project is: [DESCRIBE YOUR PROJECT IN ONE SENTENCE]. The services I use are: [SUPABASE, OPENAI, STRIPE, WHATEVER].

prompts.name: Fix a deployment that failed in red
prompts.prompt: My deployment on Vercel has failed and I need you to fix it. I don't know how to code, so don't explain theory: tell me which files to change and give them to me complete, ready to paste. I'm pasting below what shows in Vercel's Build Log. Before proposing anything, I want you to do four things in writing. One: tell me in one plain-English sentence what happened, as if explaining it to someone who's never seen code. Two: tell me whether this is a code problem, a missing environment variable problem in Vercel, a capitalization mismatch in a file name (which doesn't error on my computer but does on Vercel's servers), or a package version problem. Three: tell me exactly what I need to touch myself in the Vercel dashboard, with the literal menu and button names, if I need to touch anything at all. Four: give me the fix. If the fix involves adding or renaming an environment variable, explicitly remind me that afterward I need to go to Deployments, three dots, Redeploy, and uncheck the cache, because otherwise the change does nothing. If you don't have enough information in the log, tell me which other part of the log you need and from which line, instead of guessing. Here's the error: [PASTE THE LOG, FROM THE FIRST LINE SAYING ERROR: TO THE END].

prompts.name: Works on my computer but not on the internet
prompts.prompt: I have the classic problem and I want you to diagnose it, step by step, without me needing to understand anything. On my computer my project works perfectly. Published on Vercel, it doesn't work. What's happening exactly is: [DESCRIBE WHAT YOU SEE: BLANK PAGE, THE BUTTON DOES NOTHING, ERROR 500, THE CHAT DOESN'T RESPOND]. The address where it fails is: [PASTE THE URL]. I want you to walk me through an ordered checklist, from most to least likely, and at each point tell me what to look at, where to look with the literal Vercel menu name, and what I should see if it's fine. Cover at least these suspects: environment variables that exist in my .env.local file but not in Vercel; variables that are in Vercel but only checked for the Production environment when I'm testing a preview, or vice versa; variables added after the last deploy and therefore not applied yet; variables that need the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix for the browser to see them; values pasted with quotes, extra spaces, or a trailing line break; hardcoded addresses in the code pointing to localhost instead of my real domain; and calls that take too long and get cut off. Then tell me your main bet and give me the complete fix for that one. If you need to see any of my files, ask for it by name and I'll paste it.

prompts.name: Work with branches and use previews without breaking the site
prompts.prompt: I want to stop breaking my published site every time I try something. Explain to me and set up a way to work with branches using Vercel's previews, assuming I don't know how to code and I do everything by talking to you. First explain to me with an everyday comparison what a branch is and why my main branch, main, is the one that goes live for real while any other branch only shows up at a test address that whoever I choose can see. Then give me the full flow in numbered steps for the change I want to make, which is: [DESCRIBE THE CHANGE: REDESIGNING THE HOMEPAGE, ADDING PAYMENTS, CHANGING THE COPY]. At each step tell me literally what to ask you and what to look at on screen. Include: how to create the branch, how to find its preview address on Vercel and where it shows up, how to check the preview uses the correct environment variables and not the real production ones, what to do if opening the preview asks me to log into Vercel, how to show it to someone else, and how to merge the branch into main once I like it. End by telling me how to undo everything if I regret it after publishing, with the exact name of Vercel's button, and warning me about what that button does NOT fix.

prompts.name: Connect my own domain and understand DNS
prompts.prompt: I've bought (or I'm about to buy) the domain [MYDOMAIN.COM] and I want to connect it to my site published on Vercel, which right now is at [MYPROJECT.VERCEL.APP]. My domain is registered at [WHERE YOU BOUGHT IT: IONOS, GODADDY, NAMECHEAP, VERCEL, DINAHOSTING]. I don't know how to code and DNS sounds like gibberish to me, so explain it like it's the phone switchboard that says which number matches which name. Give me the following. One: the exact steps in Vercel, with literal menu and button names, to add the domain. Two: explain to me the two ways to do it, changing the nameservers or adding individual records, which one suits me and why, and what risk each carries if I have email working on that same domain. Three: tell me exactly which records I need to create in my registrar's panel, what each field is called there and what to put in each one, warning me that the correct values are the ones Vercel shows on screen and not whatever's in some tutorial, because they change. Four: tell me how long it takes to work and why the old site might still show during that time. Five: tell me what to do if Vercel shows Invalid Configuration. Six: tell me if I need to change any environment variable in my project now that the address is different.

words: Deploy
Publish. Every time Vercel takes your code, builds it, and puts it on the internet, that's a deploy. You'll have hundreds. They're all saved and you can go back to any of them.
Build

The roughly one-minute stretch where the machine translates your files into something a browser understands. If something's written wrong, it blows up here and never gets published. It's your safety net.
Environment variable

A named piece of data your site needs to work but that isn't written inside the code, because it's secret or because it changes from place to place. Example: the OpenAI key. Think of an envelope with a label on the outside and the password inside: the code asks for 'the OPENAI_API_KEY envelope' and Vercel hands it over.
The three environments (Production, Preview, Development)

The three places your site can run, and where each variable can have a different value. Production is the real site, the one on your domain. Preview is the test copies, one per branch. Development is your own computer. When creating a variable you choose where it applies; forget one and that's where it fails.
Branch

A parallel copy of your project where you can try things without touching what's published. The main one is called main and is the one that goes public. Any other branch only shows up at its own test address.
Preview URL
The address Vercel creates on its own for each branch, something like myapp-git-branchname-yourusername.vercel.app. Used to show a change before everyone sees it.
Rollback
Restoring your public site to a previous version with one click. It doesn't build anything, it just flips the switch. The code on GitHub stays as it was, meaning it's still broken.
Domain and DNS

The domain is the pretty name, mystore.com. DNS is the switchboard that translates that name into Vercel's machine's numeric address. When you connect a domain, what you're doing is touching that switchboard.
Function (serverless function)

A small piece of your site that isn't a page but a task: calling the AI, saving an order, sending an email. It only runs when someone asks for it, has a maximum time, and is billed per use. That's where 500 and 504 errors come from.
Log

The machine's diary. There are two: the 'Build Log', from when the site was built, saved with every deploy; and the 'Logs' or runtime logs, of what happens while people use it, which on the free plan last a short time.
matters: An environment variable doesn't exist until you redeploy. It's the rule that will save you the most time in the whole course. You can write the perfect key in Vercel and your site will keep failing exactly the same, because the version that's online was built before the key existed and won't go looking for it. After touching any variable: 'Deployments' → '⋯' → 'Redeploy'. Ignoring this means spending an hour convinced the key is wrong when the key is perfect.

Anything with NEXT_PUBLIC_ in front can be read by anyone, and anything without it the browser can't see. Both halves of this rule hurt. If you put Stripe's secret key or Supabase's service_role with the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix, anyone who opens your site can extract it and empty your database or spend your balance. If you forget the prefix on one that actually needs to be in the browser, the page comes out blank. Before accepting a change from the AI that touches variables, ask it: 'is this variable secret? why does it or doesn't it get NEXT_PUBLIC_?'

The rollback button exists and it's your safety net, but it doesn't fix the code. 'Instant Rollback' restores your site to the good version in seconds, and that's gold when people are watching. What it doesn't do is touch what's saved on GitHub. The broken code is still there, and as soon as the AI pushes the next change, the bug goes live again. The right order is always: first rollback to stop the bleeding, then actually fix it with the AI, then push again.

The free plan has real limits and the domain costs money every year. Hobby is 100 GB of traffic a month, 100 deploys a day (which run out faster than you think when you're vibe-coding and pushing twenty changes an hour), and non-commercial use: if your site makes money, Vercel will ask you to move to Pro, about €19 a month per person. Separately, buying a domain runs €12 to €25 a year depending on the extension, it auto-renews every year, and it's non-refundable. Connecting a domain you already own to Vercel is free. Before entering a card anywhere, check the price on screen, not in this guide: prices change.
ignore: Analytics, Speed Insights, and performance notes. Vercel will offer to measure visits and speed with very pretty charts. Useless while three people a day are visiting, and some of them consume from your plan. Turn them on once you have real traffic.

The Vercel CLI, Edge Config, Edge Middleware, regions, and monorepos. All of that is for people deploying from a black command-line window and managing several projects at once. You're going to do everything from the web with buttons, and it works just as well. If the AI suggests installing the CLI, tell it you prefer doing it from the dashboard.

Teams, collaborators, roles, and Marketplace integrations. While you work alone, all of that is paperwork for companies. The Integrations tab has dozens of services you can plug in with one click; almost all of them have their own price. Don't plug in anything you haven't needed yet.
